A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeQA-Score research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated results.

before.justification: V1 reports original discretization analyses, trained-model evaluations, distribution predictions, ablations, and quality-description experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds evaluations on further datasets, additional baseline comparisons, and a level-count sensitivity study.

M1.justification: The proposed model retains Gaussian soft-label construction, linear post-adjustment, the same architecture and training losses, and the same score-distribution inference procedure. Additional level-count configurations are experimental ablations, without replacing the proposed five-level method.

E1.justification: V2 substantially expands unseen-image evaluation through FLIVE's authentic images in Table 3 and three additional generated-image datasets—AIGCIQA2023, AGIN, and AGIQA-1K—in Table A4. This particularly broadens the previously single-dataset generated-image evaluation. Existing training datasets and tasks remain; AGIQA becoming AGIQA-3K is a naming clarification.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Compare2Score, which v1 discussed but did not evaluate. Appendix Table A5 also expands the multi-dataset comparison beyond Q-Align by evaluating LIQE and Compare2Score, substantially broadening the direct evidence against alternative scoring methods.

E3.justification: Table A6 introduces controlled configurations with 6, 7, 8, 10, and 12 numerical-word rating levels. Its five-level condition matches v1's Number condition in Table 7. Retained experiments have no reported changes to training budgets, splits, or metrics; KL divergence is relocated rather than dropped.

E4.justification: The new Table A6 tests sensitivity to discretization granularity by varying the number of rating levels. Existing loss, label-text, and trainable-component ablations, qualitative examples, and quality-description extensions are retained.

E5.justification: Human-rating variances and label-adjustment statistics retain their reporting practices. Neither version supplies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests for model performance.

E6.justification: New dataset, comparator, and level-count results substantially expand the empirical record. For example, the new FLIVE column reports PLCC/SRCC of 0.589/0.501 for DeQA-Score versus 0.554/0.483 for Q-Align. Table A5 also shows LIQE exceeding DeQA-Score on TID2013, 0.881/0.854 versus 0.852/0.820. Previously reported numerical results remain unchanged, including KL values moved to Table A3.

T1.justification: The mathematical assumptions and method derivations in Equations 1–9 and A1–A2 are unchanged. New Equation A3 states the standard Gaussian KL-divergence formula for an existing evaluation metric; it adds explanation rather than a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions and claims about accurate score regression, distribution prediction, and multi-dataset training. The shortened conclusion and added adjective 'pioneering' do not materially change their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds an explanation of level-count tradeoffs, elaborates how small predicted variances produce large KL divergence, and acknowledges high memory consumption. Existing co-training and small-variance limitations remain. The new claim of consistent superiority over additional baselines is broader than Table A5 supports.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly discloses 15.2G storage in bfloat16 and inference memory of 15.8G and 23.0G for batch sizes 1 and 64. These are additional resource details, without an established change to implementation. Existing training details and code/model access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Eight references are added, including sources for the additional datasets, ATTIQA, and contextual IQA and image-processing work. The related-work narrative and positioning relative to Q-Align and UNIQUE remain largely unchanged. Compare2Score and the work underlying LIQE were already cited in v1.

P1.justification: V2 combines single- and multi-dataset regression discussions in Section 5.2, condenses the conclusion, improves appendix cross-references, and adds a normalization footnote. Affiliations and acknowledgments are updated. Most prose and the overall document organization are retained.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains a comparator row and FLIVE column; Table 5's KL results become Appendix Table A3, while new Tables A4–A6 display added experiments. Existing appendix tables are renumbered and relocated. Figure 6 is restyled and Table 6's component columns are reordered, while the other figures and overall layout remain largely intact.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's Q-Align-only multi-dataset comparison, v2 provides broader competitor evidence, additional unseen-image evaluations, and a useful test of level-count sensitivity. Memory disclosure also improves assessment of deployment requirements. These address focused validation and reporting gaps. The gains are tempered by Appendix C's overly broad superiority statement: Table A5 shows LIQE ahead on TID2013 and PIPAL PLCC.
